Every time I board the high-speed rail, the same small ritual starts. I check
how many pages are left in the book I'm carrying, and I check how long the ride
is — say two to three hours. Those pages must be finished before the train
arrives. So the problem inverts itself: pages remaining divided by minutes
available gives the reading rate I must sustain, and I already know my measured
baseline speed from earlier timed sessions. If the required rate sits below my
baseline, I can relax into the text. If it sits above, I know *right now* —
not at the disappointing end of the ride — that I need to skim the case studies
and slow down only for the arguments.

It is a trivial example, and that is exactly why I keep returning to it.
Nothing about it is clever. It is just **backward derivation plus
quantification**: fix the endpoint, measure the current state, compute the
required rate, compare against a calibrated baseline. Yet most of student life
— literature reading, experiment scheduling, thesis chapters, even gym sessions
— runs on vague forward hope instead: *start, try hard, see where we land.*
The engineering move is always the inverse. Start from where you must land, and
let the arithmetic tell you what today has to look like.

## The few variables that carry everything

What makes backward derivation so effective is that it almost always exposes a
Pareto structure. Derive backward from the goal, quantify the chain, and you
find that two or three variables carry most of the outcome — the 80/20 rule
showing up, as it always does. For the train it is just reading rate. For a
cycling experiment it might be one current density and one electrolyte volume.
For a manuscript it is usually one figure and one paragraph of argument that
decide the reviewer's mood, not the other twenty pages.

Most things, I've found, *nearly solve themselves* once you backward-derive,
quantify, and isolate the few key variables. The remaining 80% of effort is
real, but it is maintenance, not leverage. The engineering discipline is
refusing to spread attention evenly across a chain whose links do not
contribute evenly.

## Automate what has become boring

The second transplant is automation, and the rule I use is simple: **anything
mature enough to be repeated identically is mature enough to be code.** The
first time you do something, do it by hand and take notes. The fifth time,
those notes have become a checklist. The fifteenth time, the checklist should
already be a script — and if it needs to run on a schedule rather than on
demand, even the humble Windows Task Scheduler is enough to make it disappear
from your conscious life entirely.

This is not about saving minutes. It is about what repetition does to
attention. A routine performed manually still occupies a slot in working
memory: did I run it, did I do the steps in order, did I forget the export
flag. A routine that runs itself occupies nothing. Piece by piece, the mature
parts of a research workflow should calcify into an assembly line, so that the
live mind is spent only where the problems are still alive.

## First principles, and the right to start over

Why insist on first principles rather than recipes? Because recipes only work
inside the conditions they were written for, and research is precisely the
activity of leaving those conditions. Owning the chain from the bottom —
knowing *why* each step exists, being able to rebuild any stage from
fundamentals — is what reduces uncertainty when the situation shifts. It is
the SpaceX posture: treat failure as an expected part of iteration, and design
everything, from day one, to be rebuilt.

Which is why the most underrated engineering habit of all is the backup. Not
backup as IT hygiene — backup as *psychology*. When every dataset, script, and
draft is versioned and restorable, risk loses most of its teeth. An experiment
can fail, a hard drive can die, a whole approach can prove wrong, and the
answer is the same: restore, rebuild, rise again. You can afford boldness
precisely because you cannot be ruined.

## Finish completely, then move on completely

The last piece is the one that took me longest to appreciate: **do things
thoroughly**. Close the loop, document the result, archive the artifacts, leave
the workspace clean. Thoroughness looks like perfectionism but functions as its
opposite — it is what lets you *stop thinking about the thing*. A task finished
at 90% keeps a background process running in your head indefinitely; a task
finished at 100%, with its backups made and its notes written, releases the
memory entirely.

And that is the real payoff of the whole transplanted paradigm. Backward
derivation removes the anxiety of not knowing whether today is enough.
Quantification replaces mood with arithmetic. Automation clears the routine
from working memory. First principles plus backups remove the fear of ruin.
Thoroughness closes each loop for good. What remains is a mind that is
genuinely, wholly available — free to turn to the next thing and commit to it
with everything, and then to tackle another mission.
